messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
The equivalence requires proving both directions of the nested closed-set intersection property.

Does completeness give a convergent sequence from the nested sets?

There exists a point x_n \in F_n for each n.

Since F_{n+1} \subset F_n, every x_m with m>n lies in F_n, so d(x_n,x_m) \le \operatorname{diam} F_n, and \operatorname{diam} F_n tends to 0 as n \to \infty.

Thus (x_n) is Cauchy, and completeness gives a limit x \in M.

Must x belong to every F_n?

For each k, the tail (x_n)_{n\ge k} lies in F_k, and closedness of F_k forces x \in F_k.

Does the reverse direction use a Cauchy sequence?

For a Cauchy sequence (y_n), the sets F_n = \overline{\{y_k : k \ge n\}} form a nested family of nonempty closed sets with F_{n+1} \subset F_n and diameters tending to 0 as n \to \infty.

Does the intersection point x force convergence of (y_n)?

For every \varepsilon, the fact that x lies in every tail closure and the Cauchy property give an N with d(x,y_n) < \varepsilon for all n \ge N.

Therefore M is complete.
